newsitem.title: USA: MUNI ISSUER FOCUS - Tampa Bucs bonds finally ready.
newsitem.headline: MUNI ISSUER FOCUS - Tampa Bucs bonds finally ready.

text.p: After 2 1/2 years of negotiation, litigation and frustration, the Tampa Sports Authority's $195.1 million revenue bond issue is finally headed to market.
Smith Barney Inc will price the negotiated issue on Tuesday, with proceeds financing construction of a new 65,000-seat stadium for the Tampa Bay Buccanneers.
"This is it," said Mike Merrill, debt manager for Florida's Hillsborough County.

The Florida Supreme Court cleared the way for the issue on Wednesday when it refused without comment to reconsider its validation of the bonds. Ecstatic county officials considered rushing to market Friday to take advantage of favorable conditions, but opted to wait until Tuesday.
"It needs a little bit more massaging in the marketplace to make sure everybody understands where the whole business of litigation is," Merrill said.
"I don't think we'll be penalized at all as long as we take some time to make sure the market understands the bonds are validated and there's no more litigation risk," he said.

The bonds are in three series, all insured. A $29.5 million series is insured by Financial Security Assurance and backed with state sales tax rebates. Florida law allows professional sports franchises to receive rebates on sales tax revenues from tickets and stadium concessions, up to $2 a year for 30 years.
A $154 million series is insured by MBIA Insurance Corp and backed with revenues from a local-option sales tax that voters approved last September.
The final $11.6 million series is insured by MBIA and backed with revenues from Hillsborough County's tourism tax.
"It's just about as straightforward as you can get," Merrill said. "Other than the litigation, it's extremely ordinary. It shouldn't have been a hard deal at all."

Bucs' owner Malcolm Glazer had threatened to move the team unless the county replaced the 29-year-old Tampa Stadium. After lengthy negotions with Glazer, Hillsborough County lawmakers asked the state Legislature in 1996 for permission to levy a tax on rental cars to fund a new stadium.

In a virulently anti-tax mood ahead of last fall's elections, legislators not only refused but suggested that any funding for the Bucs should be tied to the team's win-loss record. The ignomious Bucs have the worst record in the history of professional sports.

When an ammended bill that would have used property tax revenues died in the session, local officials hatched a last-ditch proposal to raise Hillsborough's sales tax by a half-cent. It also provided funding for badly needed school and road projects and was approved by voters in September 1996.

Stadium construction began immediately and the bonds were to be sold in November. But the deal was blocked when former Tampa Mayor William Poe sued, claiming the project would unconstitutionally use public money to benefit the private, for-profit team.
The county, City of Tampa and the Tampa Sports Authority sought bond validation, which was merged with the lawsuit.

Hillsborough County Circuit Court Judge Sam Pendino stunned the county by refusing to validate the bonds. He ruled in March that the project was essentially for private purpose because of lease provisions giving the Bucs the first $2 million in annual revenues from non-Bucs events at the stadium.

But Pendino said he would validate the bonds if the lease provision was changed. That sent the city, county and Bucs back into negotiatons and prompted Poe to take the unusual step of appealing a ruling he had won.
Poe went to the Florida Supreme Court, which reviewed the revised lease agreement and validated the bonds last month, then refused Wednesday to rehear the case.

The sports authority had only enough money to continue construction through July 1 without the bond proceeds. With all avenues of legal appeal exhausted, and the bond sale set for Tuesday, the stadium is expected to open on time on Sept. 20, 1998, Bucs spokesman Reggie Roberts said.
"We're a month ahead of schedule," Roberts said. "We're very, very, very excited."
